thread.title: Hair Of The Bear: Where Is Santa? | Seeking Alpha

author: Long-Short Manager
title: Hair Of The Bear: Where Is Santa? | Seeking Alpha
text:
Note: All graphs are sourced to Bloomberg unless specifically noted otherwise.
Introduction Based on the immediate market reaction to the results of the Fed meeting and conference, there was still some hope of much more dovish signals from the Fed that would suggest a pause was at hand. Instead, the Fed signaled that, absent significant deterioration in economic measures between now and the March meeting, we could see another hike in the Fed Funds rate. The median of the dot plots moved down a notch, suggesting that "neutral" might mean two more hikes in 2019. There was no mention of slowing down or terminating Quantitative Tightening.
The initial reaction from algos a second after 2pm was a 125 point drop in the NASDAQ, followed by other algos and some brave humans stepping in for a short rally. In human time, once the minutes had been read and the conference call listened too, the decline continued into the close. This leaves the year-to-date picture as follows:
The 1-year total return of QQQ is now -1.35%, while from the peak in August, it is -17%, a mere 3% decline (or a bad bear hair day) away from official bear market territory. Not only can we see the quivering hairs of the bear as it approaches us, but it is close enough that we can see its eyes and fangs. Speaking of FAANGs, this is how they have done this year against QQQ.
Of the FAANG pack, only Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) is not already in bear market territory, waiting for QQQ itself to cross the threshold. The rest have been leading the way, with Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ) and Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) in the lead, with Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) not far behind, all down over 25%.
A Look At Bears Past Given that the classical psychological stages of bear markets are denial, aggressive fear-based selling (often with even worse declines than in the denial phase) followed by capitulation, let's take a look at bear markets past. I'll use my personal experiences of the bear markets of the 2000 bubble correction and the 2008 financial meltdown to supply some narrative.
Let's start with 2008, when QQQ was not a direct participant in the troubles of the financial system or mortgages, but was nevertheless impacted by a wide-ranging and deep recession.
As you can see on the price and volume graph, the "denial" phase lasted from January to September of 2008, when a spring correction was fought back into the summer. Anyone who listened to "sell in May and go away..." would have done well. With the demise of Bear Stearns, quickly followed by Lehman, the dominoes started to fall and September-November saw the fear stage. Note the massive increase in volume. This is when the folks in denial began to finally throw in the towel in increasing numbers. Finally, November through March saw a drop in volume, a consolidation of the low price level, with capitulation occurring in March. Please note the slope of the recovery because we will compare it to the next graph.
In the case of 2000, QQQ was the heart of bubble territory. Denial lasted almost the entire year of 2000 and interestingly the correction started in September as well (just like this year!). To the extent that I can point to a "catalyst" (other than ridiculous valuations that just had to eventually end as there wasn't enough money in the whole world to keep it going), the one I remember most was the ruling against Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) in the anti-trust trial. The fear stage lasted a whole year through September with "capitulation" occurring sometime around there. The recovery compared to 2009 was quite shallow with a much slower recovery. In fact, QQQ did not recover its highs from 2000 during the entirety of the next bull cycle, so all of the years 2003-2008 could be viewed as one LONG bear market rally for QQQ, with true capitulation not occurring until the second bear. In fact, it was not until 2014, almost a half generation of investors later, that QQQ returned to triple digits and not until this year when it rose meaningfully (50%) above its prior bull peak.
Lessons for Now The first question that is important to ask is - how central is QQQ to the bear market dynamics? In terms of valuations, we went into this year with the indices at the third highest levels ever (behind 2000 and 1929 but above every other classic peak), but with QQQ valuations (which did not exist in 1929) almost as high as in 2000. The names and players in QQQ have changed to some extent (especially the weights - GOOG and AMZN were tiny parts of QQQ in 2000 and FB and NFLX did not exist). To the extent the bear is being driven by fundamentals rather than valuations and psychology (of course, all three always matter), QT and the Fed Funds rate apply to all companies. They apply more to companies that rely on debt for growth and whose valuation multiples rely upon that growth narrative to be supported. They apply more to companies with weak FCF dynamics that cannot rely on organic cash flows to continue to grow, making such companies' beta to economic slowdowns much more severe. This, combined with the sorts of folks who seem to invariably gravitate to such stories, explains the high beta of QQQ and especially its richest and most famous names.
In my last macro article about a month ago, in the series about momentum traders, market micro-structure and the potential for a bear, I put the odds of a bear at roughly 50/50 but suggested that the Santa Claus Rally story was continuing denial. Had this denial story succeeded in rousing investors out of the rising fear, we would have stopped at a correction. At this point, on the heels of the Fed meeting, I would move those odds to 80/20 and recommend positioning appropriately.
Another important question to ask is "how bad will this one get?". Since the denial phase has taken us to -17%, the fear phase, which is usually the more brutal, suggests that at least 35% is likely now. Given the changes in market micro-structure, it could happen faster than in the past (algos change from "denial" to "fear" mode in seconds, and too many of them "think" the same way). On the other hand, looking at individual names, many sectors are already in value territory, from energy to healthcare to consumer durables (especially housing and autos). So unlike the market-wide bubble of 2000, many sectors, if they continue to fall, will go from being already cheap to dirt cheap. Look at FedEx (NYSE: FDX ), for example. It is already pricing in a recession and we haven't entered a bear. This suggests a higher than "normal" level of dispersion in results going forward into the next bear stage.
Will we have a recession? In 2000, the recession was caused by the equity market decline and the contraction in the tech sector, which was leading massive capital spending. It was shallow, with a relatively quick recovery. In 2008, the economy was fundamentally sick, having been propped up by the cash from ill-gotten housing equity bubble gains via cash outs. So was the financial system, which supplied those ill-gotten gains via opaque instruments which magnified systemic risks. When the source of that cash, the psychology of housing bubble buying, and those financial instruments all exploded, it created an explosion that touched almost every corner of the world.
In contrast, the economy is mostly fundamentally sound. The only "ill-gotten gains" we can identify in the system are the sugar-high from the corporate tax cut and extraordinary levels of government deficit, with CLOs and lending to subprime companies a much smaller second. There are no signs of the first causing trouble yet; whether the second causes trouble or not will depend on the severity of the economic slowdown that follows these market dynamics due to the reverse wealth effect. If this slowdown is significant enough (e.g., tips us into recession), then second-order damage is possible that could deepen the bear from 35% to the traditional 40-50% deep recessionary bear territory.
Finally, what are the catalysts that could make the bear more shallow than the 35-40% indicated by history? A Fed pause in March combined with the end of the trade war could easily mark the end of the bear market. However, given market structure, it is also possible that fear through capitulation will have entirely been completed by March. This suggests that forecasts of a bear market "later in 2019" were potentially part of the cycle of denial, allowing folks to continue partying well past last call.
Hopefully, whatever moves you were going to make to position yourself have already been made. If they have not, do them now - doing so any later will increase the odds that you will be one of the sellers during the capitulation phase, which is the worst place to be. Doing otherwise requires intestinal fortitude of the highest order.
Disclosure: I am/we are short NFLX, AMZN. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
